# A Fresh Start for the Nation's Finances: Abolishing Income Tax and Adopting a Single Flat Consumption Tax

## Executive Summary

The income tax is a relic of a bygone age. It is complicated, intrusive and punishing, and it taxes the one thing a healthy economy needs most: work. This white paper sets out a bold and simple alternative. We propose abolishing the federal income tax in its entirety, along with payroll taxes, capital gains taxes and the estate tax, and replacing the whole edifice with a single flat consumption tax levied on retail sales. The plan is simple enough to explain on a postcard, fair enough that everyone pays the same rate, and powerful enough to unleash a wave of growth, savings and prosperity. The time for half-measures has passed. The nation deserves a tax system worthy of a free people.

## 1. The Problem with the Income Tax

Few institutions are as universally loathed as the income tax. Citizens spend billions of hours and billions of dollars every year simply trying to comply with it. The tax code runs to many thousands of pages, an impenetrable thicket of brackets, deductions, credits, phase-outs and exemptions that no ordinary person can hope to understand. An entire industry of accountants, lawyers and lobbyists exists only to navigate, exploit and perpetuate this complexity.

Worse, the income tax punishes exactly the behaviour a prosperous society should reward. Every additional hour worked, every promotion earned, every business expanded is met by the taxman's hand reaching deeper into the citizen's pocket. The income tax is, quite literally, a tax on productivity. It discourages effort, it discourages investment, and it discourages the saving on which all future growth depends. A system that penalises work and thrift is a system designed for stagnation.

The income tax is also an instrument of surveillance. To enforce it, the government must know what every citizen earns, from whom, and how. It must track wages, dividends, interest, capital gains and gifts. This is an extraordinary intrusion into private life, one we have come to accept only through long habituation. A free people should not have to file an annual confession of their financial affairs to the state.

## 2. The Solution: A Single Flat Consumption Tax

Our proposal is elegant in its simplicity. Abolish the income tax. Abolish the payroll tax. Abolish the capital gains tax and the estate tax. In their place, levy a single flat tax on the final retail sale of goods and services. Every purchase is taxed once, at the same rate, with no exceptions and no loopholes.

The advantages are immediate and obvious.

**Simplicity.** The plan can be described on a postcard. There are no brackets, no deductions, no credits, no annual filing for individuals. Citizens would never again fill out a tax return. The thousands of pages of the tax code would be replaced by a single rate.

**Fairness.** Everyone pays the same rate on what they spend. There is no special treatment for the well-connected, no carve-outs for favoured industries, no army of lobbyists carving loopholes into the code. The billionaire and the bus driver pay the identical rate at the till. What could be fairer than that?

**Growth.** By removing the tax on work, saving and investment, the plan would unleash the productive energies of the nation. People would keep their entire pay cheque. Businesses would invest without the distorting drag of the corporate and capital gains taxes. Savings would surge, because saving would no longer be punished. Economists have long agreed that consumption taxes are more pro-growth than income taxes, and the logic is undeniable.

**Freedom.** The government would no longer need to know what anyone earns. The surveillance apparatus of the income tax could be dismantled. The relationship between citizen and state would be transformed from one of suspicion to one of trust.

## 3. Why a Flat Rate Is the Fairest of All

Some will object that a flat rate is unfair because it does not rise with income. This objection rests on a confusion. Fairness does not mean treating people differently; it means treating them the same. A flat consumption tax does exactly that. Everyone faces the identical rate. The person who spends more, pays more, automatically and in proportion. A wealthy family that buys a yacht pays vastly more tax than a young couple buying groceries, without any need for brackets or means-testing. The tax is therefore progressive in its effect while remaining beautifully simple in its design.

Indeed, the flat rate is the only truly equal tax. Graduated income taxes single out the successful for higher rates, which is a form of punishment for achievement. A flat consumption tax treats every citizen as an equal before the law of taxation, exactly as a just society should.

## 4. Unleashing Economic Growth

The growth case for this reform is overwhelming. Consider the incentives. Under the income tax, the reward for extra work is reduced by the marginal rate. Under a pure consumption tax, work is not taxed at all; only spending is. The incentive to earn is fully restored.

The same logic applies to saving and investment. The income tax taxes the return on savings, so it penalises the patient and rewards the spendthrift. A consumption tax does the opposite: money that is saved and invested is never taxed until it is finally spent, if it ever is. This is precisely the incentive structure a growing economy needs. Nations that save and invest grow; nations that consume and borrow stagnate. Our plan rebuilds the foundations of long-term prosperity.

Capital would also flood into the country. With no income tax, no capital gains tax and no corporate tax, the nation would become the most attractive destination for investment in the world. Factories, headquarters and entrepreneurs would relocate to take advantage of the most favourable tax environment anywhere. The resulting boom in jobs and wages would lift every citizen.

The historical record supports optimism. Periods of lower taxation have generally coincided with stronger growth, and the most dynamic economies tend to be those that tax consumption rather than income. The direction of the evidence is clear, and it points squarely towards our proposal.

## 5. Setting the Rate

A natural question is what rate would be required to replace the revenue currently raised by the income tax. The answer is reassuringly modest. Because the consumption base is broad, covering nearly all spending in the economy, even a single-digit-into-low-double-digit rate would raise enormous sums. Once the growth effects of the reform take hold, the expanding economy would generate still more revenue at any given rate, allowing the rate itself to fall over time. A tax system that becomes cheaper as the economy grows is a virtuous circle that the income tax could never achieve.

We are confident that a moderate flat rate would fully fund the legitimate functions of government while leaving citizens far better off than they are today. The exact figure can be settled by technical experts during implementation; the principle is what matters, and the principle is sound.

## 6. Answering the Critics

Critics will raise objections. Let us dispatch the main ones.

*It will hurt the poor.* On the contrary. The poor currently bear the hidden weight of payroll taxes and the embedded cost of corporate taxes passed on in higher prices. Abolish those, and prices for many goods would actually fall. The poor would also keep their entire pay cheque, with nothing withheld. They would be among the biggest winners.

*It cannot raise enough revenue.* This worry ignores the breadth of the consumption base and the growth dividend described above. A broad base at a moderate rate raises ample revenue, and a growing economy raises more.

*People will evade it.* Every tax invites some evasion, but a single-rate retail tax is far simpler to administer than the labyrinthine income tax, with its endless opportunities for avoidance through deductions and shelters. Simplicity is the enemy of evasion.

*The transition will be disruptive.* Any reform involves change, but the destination is so superior that temporary adjustment is a price well worth paying. Bold reforms are never achieved by those who fear the first step.

*It concentrates too much power in a single rate.* Some worry that relying on one tax makes revenue volatile or gives politicians a single dial to abuse. But a single visible rate is in fact the best discipline of all: when every citizen pays the same posted rate at the till, any attempt to raise it is felt immediately and universally, which makes increases politically costly and therefore rare. Compare that with the income tax, where rates can be nudged upward through obscure changes to brackets and deductions that few notice. Transparency is a safeguard, not a danger.

These objections, examined honestly, dissolve on contact with the facts. The case against reform is a case for the indefensible status quo. Every one of these worries assumes that the present system works tolerably well and that change is the thing to be feared. The truth is the reverse: it is the status quo that is failing the nation every single day, quietly and expensively, and it is reform that offers relief. The burden of proof lies not with those who would fix a broken system but with those who would defend it.

## 7. The Burden of the Current System in Detail

It is worth dwelling on just how heavy the present system is, because familiarity has bred acceptance of the intolerable. Consider first the sheer scale of compliance. The hours that citizens and businesses devote each year to record-keeping, form-filling and the hiring of professionals represent an enormous deadweight loss, productive time and money diverted into the unproductive task of working out what one owes. None of this effort builds a road, teaches a child or invents a product. It exists solely to feed the machinery of the income tax.

Consider next the distortions woven through the code. Because the income tax taxes different activities at different rates, it nudges citizens and firms into choices they would not otherwise make. People are pushed towards debt, because interest is treated favourably, and away from saving, because returns are taxed. Firms structure themselves around the tax code rather than around what makes commercial sense. Whole categories of economic decision are warped by the desire to minimise tax rather than to maximise genuine value. A clean consumption tax, falling on all final sales at one rate, would remove these distortions at a stroke. The market, not the tax accountant, would once again allocate capital.

Consider, finally, the corrosive effect on civic trust. A code so complex that no citizen can understand it, so riddled with special provisions that the well-advised pay less than the honest, breeds cynicism about government itself. People reasonably suspect that the system is rigged in favour of those who can afford the cleverest advisers. A single, transparent rate that everyone can see and understand would do more to restore faith in the fairness of government than a thousand pious speeches. Simplicity is not merely an administrative convenience; it is a democratic virtue.

These burdens are not abstractions. They fall on every household and every business, every year, and they compound over a lifetime. A reform that lifted them would be among the most consequential improvements in the daily life of citizens that any government could deliver. That alone should command the attention of every serious lawmaker.

## 8. International Lessons

The world offers encouraging examples of the direction we propose. Across the developed world, governments have come to rely heavily on broad-based consumption taxes, recognising their efficiency and their gentle treatment of saving and investment. Value-added taxes, a close cousin of our proposal, now form a pillar of public finance on every continent. The trend is unmistakable: as economies modernise, they lean ever more on taxing what people consume rather than what they earn. We propose simply to follow this logic to its clean and natural conclusion, sweeping away the income tax altogether rather than letting two systems coexist in expensive parallel.

Some jurisdictions have gone further and prospered. Places with no income tax at all have become magnets for talent, capital and enterprise. Workers flock to keep their full pay, and companies relocate to escape the punishing rates levied elsewhere. The lesson is plain. Where the income tax is light or absent, prosperity follows. Our plan would extend that advantage to the entire nation.

Critics may point out that the countries leaning on consumption taxes typically retain their income taxes too, rather than abolishing them. That is true, but it reflects timidity and the dead weight of entrenched bureaucracy, not sound economics. The fact that no large nation has yet had the courage to abolish the income tax outright is an argument for leadership, not for caution. Someone must go first, and the rewards will accrue to the bold.

## 9. A Phased Path to Implementation

A reform of this magnitude need not happen overnight, and we envisage a smooth and confident transition. In the first phase, the consumption tax would be enacted and the income tax rates would begin to fall in step, so that citizens feel the relief immediately. In the second phase, the payroll, capital gains and estate taxes would be folded into the new system. In the final phase, the income tax would be repealed entirely and its enforcement machinery wound down, returning to citizens the time and money they once spent on compliance.

Throughout the transition, the expanding economy would cushion any short-term adjustment. As growth accelerates, revenues would rise, smoothing the path and allowing fine adjustments to the rate. The administrative simplicity of the new system would also free up resources currently consumed by enforcement of the old one. We are confident that a determined government could complete the transition within a single decade, leaving behind a tax system fit for the century ahead.

Concerns about those who have already paid income tax on savings that they will now spend under a consumption tax, and who might feel taxed twice, can be addressed with sensible transitional reliefs. The details are technical and need not detain us here; the point is that no genuine obstacle stands between the nation and this superior system, only a failure of nerve.

## 10. Conclusion: The Time Is Now

The income tax has failed. It is complex, punishing, intrusive and unloved. It taxes work, penalises saving, funds an industry of compliance and turns the state into a snoop. We can do better, and the path is clear. A single flat consumption tax would be simple, fair, pro-growth and respectful of liberty. It would let citizens keep what they earn, reward thrift, attract investment from around the world and restore trust between the people and their government.

This is not a timid proposal, and it is not meant to be. The nation faces a choice between a discredited past and a prosperous future. We urge lawmakers to seize the moment, abolish the income tax, and give the country the simple, fair and growth-friendly tax system that a free and ambitious people deserve. The postcard is ready. All that is needed is the courage to mail it.
